bull_case: Persistent Earth observation is shifting geospatial intelligence from episodic tasking to continuous monitoring. Planet's daily global coverage, expanding high-resolution/hyperspectral fleet and sovereign programs position it to help define this category.
bear_case: Demand can remain lumpy and government-heavy, while national constellations and commercial rivals may narrow the scarcity value of imagery. Structural demand growth does not guarantee Planet captures the economics.
thesis: Planet is a structural leader rather than a passive space-cycle beneficiary. Its core change is moving Earth observation from occasional image purchases toward persistent monitoring and machine-readable longitudinal data. FY27 Q2 growth, 98% recurring ACV, large RPO/backlog, Pelican/Tanager deployment and new sovereign programs support 5–10 year durability. Leadership is credible but not monopolistic: customer concentration, sovereign procurement and expanding competing constellations keep the score below exceptional.

evidence.claim: Planet describes itself as operating the largest Earth-observation fleet and is built around imaging the world every day, enabling persistent rather than episodic monitoring.
FY27 Q2 revenue grew 58% YoY, recurring ACV was 98%, RPO was $753.1M and backlog $814.9M.
Planet had 10 high-resolution Pelican satellites on orbit and shipped Tanager-2 plus 18 SuperDoves, broadening resolution, spectral and refresh capability.
FY2026 NDR was 116% and NDR including winbacks 118%, indicating existing customers expanded spend during the structural adoption phase.

counterevidence: Three customers represented 17%, 11% and 10% of Q2 revenue, so recent growth is not yet broadly distributed.
Governments and large enterprises can multi-source imagery from commercial and sovereign constellations.
Satellite replacement, launch availability and regulation create physical bottlenecks absent from pure software platforms.
Raw imagery can commoditize even while the overall geospatial-intelligence market expands.
unknowns: Long-run market share in high-frequency commercial Earth observation.
Economics of sovereign satellite-service programs after full deployment.
Whether AI applications materially expand non-geospatial user adoption.
Competitive response from national and private constellations.

uncertainties.rationale: Persistent monitoring demand is well evidenced across government and commercial use cases.
Planet is a leader, but precise share and pricing-power data are limited.
Multi-sourcing, sovereign competition and physical fleet economics remain meaningful.

falsifiers: Recurring ACV, NDR and RPO weaken together for several periods despite industry demand growth.
Competitors achieve comparable cadence and data quality at lower cost, eroding Planet's differentiation.
Sovereign demand proves episodic rather than creating durable recurring programs.

key_kpis.name: Recurring ACV / NDR
key_kpis.threshold: Recurring mix remains near 95%+ and NDR stays above 100%

key_kpis.name: RPO/backlog conversion
key_kpis.threshold: Contracted demand converts without margin deterioration

key_kpis.name: Fleet capability and utilization
key_kpis.threshold: Pelican/Tanager deployment expands paid use cases faster than fleet cost

next_checks: FY27 Q3 recurring metrics and RPO conversion

subscores.rationale: Continuous monitoring and geospatial intelligence have multi-year structural demand across defense, climate, agriculture and infrastructure.
Planet's daily global fleet and archive materially shape the persistent-monitoring category.
Multiple end markets buffer demand, but competing constellations and government procurement constrain durability.
